texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Q: I'm considering venturing into product management after being a software engineer for 3 years. Primarily, because I feel I would enjoy it more (based on my perception at least). What are some markers I should look for?
texts.text: Q: I'm considering venturing into product management after being a software engineer for 3 years. Primarily, because I feel I would enjoy it more (based on my perception at least). What are some markers I should look for?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I switched from engineering to product about ten years into my engineering career, and looking back it was one of the best decisions of my life.
texts.text: I switched from engineering to product about ten years into my engineering career, and looking back it was one of the best decisions of my life.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Though I loved programming, frankly, I was a mediocre engineer. I got my work done, but I knew I was never going to be an amazing engineer. Especially when I compared myself to many engineers I knew. I also often found myself doing (and enjoying) the PM’y work on teams I was on. At one point our head of product pulled me aside and said: “Do you want to be a product manager? You should be a product manager.”
texts.text: Though I loved programming, frankly, I was a mediocre engineer. I got my work done, but I knew I was never going to be an amazing engineer. Especially when I compared myself to many engineers I knew. I also often found myself doing (and enjoying) the PM’y work on teams I was on. At one point our head of product pulled me aside and said: “Do you want to be a product manager? You should be a product manager.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It was a difficult decision at the time. Changing career paths, particularly into a career full of soft-skills which I was uncertain I’d be any good at, while also letting my very-concrete-and-highly-valued coding skills atrophy (which they definitely did) was frightening. Initially I pushed for a hybrid PM+engineer role (why choose, I’ll do both!), but quickly learned that as a company grows, you need to fit into an org bucket. And so I chose product management.
texts.text: It was a difficult decision at the time. Changing career paths, particularly into a career full of soft-skills which I was uncertain I’d be any good at, while also letting my very-concrete-and-highly-valued coding skills atrophy (which they definitely did) was frightening. Initially I pushed for a hybrid PM+engineer role (why choose, I’ll do both!), but quickly learned that as a company grows, you need to fit into an org bucket. And so I chose product management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I still miss a lot about being an engineer (e.g. the immediate feedback, the satisfaction of building, getting into flow states – not a thing when you’re a PM), but, again, it was one of the best decisions of my life. I love being at the center of the action, talking to customers, thinking about the bigger picture, rallying the team, and working with tons of different types of people. It’s not for everyone, but it was right for me.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To help you in your decision-making process, let’s first make sure you understand what you actually do day-to-day as a PM, and then I’ll share my advice for thinking through your decision.

texts.orig: As a product manager, your days are made up of three types of work:
texts.text: As a product manager, your days are made up of three types of work:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Talking to customers, understanding their needs and pain points
texts.text: Talking to customers, understanding their needs and pain points

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Talking to internal stakeholders, understanding what’s important to them
texts.text: Talking to internal stakeholders, understanding what’s important to them

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Reviewing the latest data and user research, crafting new questions to answer through data and research
texts.text: Reviewing the latest data and user research, crafting new questions to answer through data and research

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Running brainstorms to capture new ideas
texts.text: Running brainstorms to capture new ideas

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Developing a strategy and vision for your product
texts.text: Developing a strategy and vision for your product

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Helping estimate timelines and set deadlines
texts.text: Helping estimate timelines and set deadlines

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Checking-in with team members to understand what’s behind, and ahead of, schedule
texts.text: Checking-in with team members to understand what’s behind, and ahead of, schedule

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Helping make tradeoff decisions, when planning and later when behind schedule
texts.text: Helping make tradeoff decisions, when planning and later when behind schedule

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Unblocking your team members by helping decisions get made, getting everyone the resources they need, and making sure each team member is clear on their priorities
texts.text: Unblocking your team members by helping decisions get made, getting everyone the resources they need, and making sure each team member is clear on their priorities

texts.label: list_item

texts.text: Doing quality assurance, catching and reporting bugs

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Aligning your team around a single set of priorities
texts.text: Aligning your team around a single set of priorities

texts.label: list_item

texts.text: Aligning your team around a clear strategy and vision

texts.text: Aligning your team around goals and KPIs

texts.text: Getting (and maintaining) buy-in on your priorities, strategy, and vision from external stakeholders

texts.text: Building relationships with team members and stakeholders

texts.orig: Should you pursue product management (as an engineer)
texts.text: Should you pursue product management (as an engineer)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ask yourself these questions to see which bucket you fall into more.
texts.text: Ask yourself these questions to see which bucket you fall into more.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You’re more excited about solving business challenges (e.g. strategy, growth, positioning), and customer challenges, than technical challenges
texts.text: You’re more excited about solving business challenges (e.g. strategy, growth, positioning), and customer challenges, than technical challenges

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You often have strong opinions about the user experience
texts.text: You often have strong opinions about the user experience

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Teammates often agree with your product feedback
texts.text: Teammates often agree with your product feedback

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You enjoy being at the center of the action, vs. on your own, heads-down working
texts.text: You enjoy being at the center of the action, vs. on your own, heads-down working

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You could see yourself being happy never coding professionally again
texts.text: You could see yourself being happy never coding professionally again

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You look forward to collaborating with non-engineer stakeholders
texts.text: You look forward to collaborating with non-engineer stakeholders

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You feel like you’re a mediocre engineer, and aren’t motivated to put in the time to become significantly better
texts.text: You feel like you’re a mediocre engineer, and aren’t motivated to put in the time to become significantly better

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You expect to finally run the show — most of your time will be spent aligning engineers like yourself, along with designers, researchers, execs, etc.
texts.text: You expect to finally run the show — most of your time will be spent aligning engineers like yourself, along with designers, researchers, execs, etc.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You think it’ll be an easier career path — there are far fewer PM roles than engineering roles
texts.text: You think it’ll be an easier career path — there are far fewer PM roles than engineering roles

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You can’t imagine not coding — once you’re a PM you’ll only have time to code on nights and weekends
texts.text: You can’t imagine not coding — once you’re a PM you’ll only have time to code on nights and weekends

texts.label: text
texts.orig: — as a PM, you need to be good at finding your joy in long-term outcomes
texts.text: — as a PM, you need to be good at finding your joy in long-term outcomes

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You expect to make more money — PMs and engineers make about the same amount of money
texts.text: You expect to make more money — PMs and engineers make about the same amount of money

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Shadow a PM for a day. See what the job is really like.
texts.text: Shadow a PM for a day. See what the job is really like.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Don’t rush into it. You’re only three years into your career, and having deeper engineering experience will only help you in the PM role.
texts.text: Don’t rush into it. You’re only three years into your career, and having deeper engineering experience will only help you in the PM role.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Finally, if you’re feeling the pull to try product management, and you have the opportunity, I’d go for it. It’s not a one-way door, and having a chance to get into product management is a rare thing.
texts.text: Finally, if you’re feeling the pull to try product management, and you have the opportunity, I’d go for it. It’s not a one-way door, and having a chance to get into product management is a rare thing.

texts.orig: Good luck, and let me know how it goes!
